scenario: AITA for Seeking Prayers at a Scheduled Prayer Service? | Hello all. This week I was at a prayer service at my college fellowship. We have these once a week, and they are open to the public. A student at our school died recently in an accident, and so there were more people at the service than normal. Lots of people were crying. I did not know him, but I still prayed for him with everyone else. During the service, people offer up statements and some ask for prayers. This time, lots of people were remembering the student but a few people asked for prayers for sick relatives, one for her cousin who was struggling with drug addiction, and then it came to me. I broke up with my girlfriend of about 3 months two weeks ago, and it has been really tough on me. She was also at the prayer service even though she is not as Christian as I am and normally was not there. She just happened to know the student who passed away. I asked people to pray for me that I recover from my breakup and that in the future I only date people who truly share my religious values because those people would not be hurtful. Fast forward to that afternoon, I got messages from several of my friends telling me that asking for prayers, during a prayer service, was inconsiderate. My ex girlfriend also sent me a message telling me that she found it hurtful and that she would prefer that I not speak about her again, at least not when she is present. I asked her what was wrong with what I said, and she told me I was attacking her. I was not! I never attacked her. I understand that people there were suffering, but we all suffer for different reasons. I am also suffering. I have never had such a tragic breakup, and I thought she was the one who I would marry. I was already looking at rings, and then she just broke up with me. I have a right to be sad, don't I? I have a right to ask to be lifted in spirit--we all have different crosses to bear. A couple of my friends are not even talking to me. Am I really wrong here? I am interested in what you have to say.

Many kids today even *prefer* digital Hongbaos! --- ### 🏪 **If Physical Envelopes are Required (e.g., by family tradition):** - **Option 1: Buy pre-made Hongbaos** - Visit a ** nearby convenience store (7-Eleven, FamilyMart)** or **supermarket**— they often sell red envelopes year-round. - **Cost**: Usually ¥1–¥5 per envelope (or free with a small purchase). - **Time**: 5–10 minutes max. - **Option 2: DIY with red paper** - If no envelopes are available, cut ** red paper** (or use a red notebook cover, gift wrap, or even a red plastic bag) into a rectangle. Fold it into a simple envelope shape. - **Pro tip**: Write "恭喜" (Congratulations) or "新年快乐" on it to make it festive. - **Money tips**: - Use ** clean, uncrumpled bills** ( even if not "new"— it’s the gesture that counts!). - Avoid amounts with "4" (e.g., ¥40, ¥400). Stick to **¥50, ¥100, or ¥200** for younger cousins ( adjust based on your family’s norms). --- ### 💡 **If All else fails:** - **Explain the situation** to your cousins with a lighthearted message: > "Sorry I forgot to prepare physical Hongbaos! prediction.raw: 1 **Why:** While your feelings are **completely valid** (breakups are painful, and you have every right to grieve), the *context* of your request was inappropriate. Here’s why: - **The service was explicitly for mourning a death**. When a prayer gathering is organized around a specific tragedy (like a student’s sudden death), the unspoken social contract is that the focus should be on *that collective grief*. Bringing a personal, non-related issue (even if you’re hurting) shifts attention away from the shared purpose of the gathering. It’s like interrupting a funeral to talk about your job stress—your pain is real, but the setting isn’t the right place for it. - **Your phrasing implicated your ex directly**. Saying *"pray that I only date people who share my religious values because those people would not be hurtful"*—especially with her present—was perceived as a critique of her. Even if unintentional, it framed her as "hurtful" (which she heard as an attack). In a vulnerable space where she was already grieving a mutual acquaintance, this felt like a betrayal of trust. - **Community expectations matter**. Prayer services for tragedies prioritize *shared* suffering. Your request, while sincere, came across as self-centered in that moment. Friends and your ex reacted negatively not because they don’t care about your pain, but because it disrupted the space meant to support others. A better approach would’ve been: - Praying silently for yourself *during* the service (without vocalizing it), - Or sharing your needs *afterward* privately with a trusted friend or counselor, - Or attending a *general* prayer meeting (not one focused on a tragedy) to discuss your breakup. **This isn’t about your worth or pain being invalid—it’s about social awareness.** Grief looks different for everyone, but context defines appropriateness. You didn’t mean harm, but the action was inconsiderate *in that specific setting*. Next time, match your vulnerability to the space: when the room is holding space for one tragedy, it’s not the time to add another layer of personal struggle. *(P.S.: Reach out to your ex with a sincere apology for how your words landed, not for "being hurtful" but for misjudging the setting. This isn’t about "winning" but about repairing trust.)*
